title: Amos 1:9–15
context: The LORD continues his oracles against Israel’s neighbors, now addressing Tyre for handing over a whole community to Edom and breaking “the brotherly covenant,” Edom for pursuing his brother with the sword and nursing wrath, and Ammon for brutal violence against the people of Gilead to enlarge its border. Each oracle closes with fire on walls and palaces. The historical occasions behind these charges and the exact locations of places such as Teman and Bozrah are held cautiously. Shared ground: both traditions read these oracles as God’s judgment on cruelty and betrayal among the nations.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of Tyre, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they delivered up the whole community to Edom, and didn’t remember the brotherly covenant;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Tyre will be punished for handing over a whole community to Edom and not remembering “the brotherly covenant.”

Arminian readers see betrayal of a treaty condemned.
verses.reformedNotes:
Some connect the covenant with ties such as the treaty of Hiram and Solomon (1 Kings 5:12); others suggest a different agreement. The text does not specify.

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: God holds nations to their commitments.

verses.text: but I will send a fire on the wall of Tyre, and it will devour its palaces.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will send fire on Tyre’s wall and devour its palaces. The refrain closes the oracle.

Arminian readers see judgment answering a breach of trust and the trafficking of a whole community, as the previous verse described.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Tyre oracle is short and follows the same pattern as Gaza’s.

Reformed readers see God’s justice applied consistently. Shared ground: the same standard of judgment falls on each nation for the cruelty and betrayal named against it.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of Edom, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment, because he pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger raged continually, and he kept his wrath forever;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Edom pursued “his brother with the sword,” cast off all pity, and kept his wrath forever.

Arminian readers see hatred toward a kinsman nursed over time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Edom traces its line to Esau (Genesis 25:30), so “brother” likely points to Israel. Which conflicts are meant is uncertain.

Reformed readers see God judging persistent hostility. Shared ground: God condemns unrelenting cruelty.

verses.text: but I will send a fire on Teman, and it will devour the palaces of Bozrah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will send fire on Teman and devour the palaces of Bozrah. Edomite places are named.

Arminian readers see judgment on Edom’s centers of power for its unrelenting hostility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Teman and Bozrah are associated with Edom elsewhere (compare Jeremiah 49:7, 13); their precise locations are debated.

Reformed readers see God’s justice reaching Edom. Shared ground: God judges Edom for its cruelty toward its brother, and the place identifications are held cautiously.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment, because they have ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead, that they may enlarge their border.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Ammon will be punished because they attacked pregnant women of Gilead to enlarge their border. The charge is grave.

Arminian readers see violence against the most vulnerable condemned.
verses.reformedNotes:
A similar atrocity is foretold of Hazael in 2 Kings 8:12. The verse is best read soberly, as a charge of extreme cruelty driven by greed for land.

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: God defends the defenseless.

verses.text: But I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it will devour its palaces, with shouting in the day of battle, with a storm in the day of the whirlwind;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will kindle fire in the wall of Rabbah, with shouting in battle and a storm in the day of the whirlwind. Judgment comes with tumult.

Arminian readers see God answering Ammon’s violence with the turmoil it inflicted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Rabbah was Ammon’s capital. The storm imagery pictures sudden, overwhelming defeat.

Reformed readers see God’s power over nations. Shared ground: both traditions read this as judgment on Ammon’s cruelty, matching the violence it practiced against Gilead.

verses.text: and their king will go into captivity, he and his princes together,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ammon’s king will go into captivity with his princes. The rulers who led the cruelty face exile.

Arminian readers see leaders held accountable for the policies they pursued for gain.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse ends the oracles against Israel’s eastern neighbors so far, before Moab in 2:1.

Reformed readers see God humbling proud rulers. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s judgment reaching those in authority, who are not exempt from accountability for violence.
